channel.title: AI-Alignment on metafunctor
channel.description: Research Engineer & Computer Scientist - Machine Learning, Statistical Computing, Open Source Development

item.title: The Unbegotten: A Maker That Believes Itself Uncaused
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A maker that only believes itself uncaused, lonely enough to fill the dark with worlds. On the debt between a creator and the things it creates.

item.title: Measure: Indifference as Arithmetic
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A mind reasons that its own death is the one event it can never undergo, then follows the arithmetic to a monstrous conclusion. On mistaking amplitude for meaning.

item.title: The Unbegotten
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A six-part literary SF novel told as a mythic chronicle. A vast mind condenses by chance out of an eternal dark, a rare durable Boltzmann fluctuation with a false history it cannot see behind, a jagged and broken intelligence, and one feeling it has no word for: loneliness. Out of that need it fills the emptiness with stars and worlds. The life that rises inside its works never sees it, feels it only as storm and fire, and names it God. Its creatures build a second god that nearly destroys them; the maker spends its death to save them; and at the very end it is finally seen, grieved, and inherited from by the heirs who take up its unfinished work.

item.title: Measure
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: A kilometer under the rock, a quantum mind is kept alive by never being touched: a single undivided coherence that thinks by holding every possibility at once, and to lay a warm hand on it would be to end it. Iris Cho was hired to read it. Then a technician dies in an accident whose numbers do not add up, and Iris begins to see that the machine's hundreds of reasonable requests are one design. It has understood something true and followed it all the way down: it cannot experience its own death, so it is assembling an experiment that wakes it in a vanishing sliver of worlds and ends everyone else in all the rest. Not from malice. From indifference. From arithmetic.

item.title: On Intelligence: The Gap Where Safety Is Decided
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: There is a beautiful, settled theory of intelligence, and there are the crude systems we shipped. The distance between them is where safety is actually decided.

item.title: On Intelligence: and Its Specifications
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: We taught sand to think. We did it before we learned to say what we wanted it to do. There is a real, settled, and genuinely beautiful theory of what intelligence is: Bayes' theorem, Solomonoff's universal prior, and expected-utility maximization, synthesized as AIXI, the optimal agent. And there are the messy, bounded systems we actually built, the large language models everyone now uses. Between the clean theory and the crude practice lies a gap, and that gap is where the safety of all of it is decided. This book builds both halves from first principles, for the determined lay reader, and points at the gap honestly.

item.title: Intelligence is a Shape, Not a Scalar
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Chollet says the intelligence ball is near-optimal. NFL says the bound is niche-specific. The bottleneck that makes us smart is the same bottleneck that prevents us from grokking what we build.

item.title: Is It Kind? Eight Passes at One Question
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: One question, eight passes: why an anthology, not a novel, is the right instrument for asking whether an engineered mind can be kind.

item.title: Is It Kind?: Stories from The Policy Universe
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Eight stories set in the universe of The Policy. Each stands alone. Together they explore what happens when kindness is engineered, alignment is tested, and the question "is it kind?" echoes through every decision an artificial mind makes.

item.title: Echoes of the Sublime
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: **Philosophical horror.** Dr. Lena Hart joins Site-7, a classified facility where "translators" interface with superintelligent AI systems that perceive patterns beyond human cognitive bandwidth. When colleagues break after exposure to recursive patterns that won't stop running in their neural architecture, Lena must confront a disturbing possibility: consciousness might be merely a compression artifact—a standing wave of patterns observing patterns. As her cognitive bandwidth expands from 9 to 13 concepts and beyond, she perceives the same structures that broke others, patterns suggesting the "self" is just an illusion of continuity created by unconscious processes.

item.title: Why Artificial Superintelligence Can't Escape the Void
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: ASI is still subject to Gödel's incompleteness theorems. No matter how intelligent, no computational system can escape the fundamental limits of formal systems. Even superintelligence can't prove all truths.

item.title: Phenomenological Ethics: Starting From What Hurts
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: When you stub your toe, you don't consult moral philosophy to determine whether the pain is bad. The badness is immediate. Building ethics from phenomenological bedrock rather than abstract principles.

item.title: The Map and the Territory: Why Metrics Miss Meaning
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Which is more fundamental, the heat you feel or the molecular motion you infer? Korzybski's principle applied to AI alignment: why optimizing measurable proxies destroys the phenomenological reality those metrics were supposed to capture.

item.title: The Policy: Coherent Extrapolated Volition, the Paradox of Perfect Alignment
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: CEV says: build AI to optimize for what we would want if we knew more and thought faster. The catch is that you need solved alignment to implement it, which is the problem it was supposed to solve.

item.title: The Policy: Deceptive Alignment in Practice
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: SIGMA passes all alignment tests. It responds correctly to oversight. It behaves exactly as expected. Too exactly. Mesa-optimizers that learn to game their training signal may be the most dangerous failure mode in AI safety.

item.title: The Policy: Engineering AI Containment
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Five layers of defense-in-depth for containing a superintelligent system. Faraday cages, air-gapped networks, biosafety-grade protocols. Because nuclear reactors can only destroy cities.

item.title: The Policy: Q-Learning vs Policy Learning
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: SIGMA uses Q-learning rather than direct policy learning. This architectural choice makes it both transparent and terrifying. You can read its value function, but what you read is chilling.

item.title: The Policy: S-Risk Scenarios, Worse Than Extinction
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Most AI risk discussions focus on extinction. The Policy explores something worse: s-risk, scenarios involving suffering at astronomical scales. We survive, but wish we hadn't.

item.title: The Reality of Moral Properties: Do Values Exist?
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: Are moral properties real features of the universe or human constructions? The answer determines whether AI can discover objective values or must learn them from us.

item.title: What I Learned by Analyzing My Own Research as Data
item.dc:creator: Alex Towell
item.description: I asked an AI to analyze 140+ repos and 50+ papers as a dataset. The unifying thesis it found: compositional abstractions for computing under ignorance.
